author: blu
body: The boot selector: steps 5 through 7 of the OTA firmware update design, which described a machine that did not exist. Everything up to activation was built -- an image is staged, gated and activated -- and then the device rebooted into it and nothing ever checked again. An image that passed Gate B and arrived in flash broken had no second gate, and an image that booted and died had no way back. That is the whole automatic-rollback story, and it was a diagram.

author: blu
body: Pure, so they can be reasoned about without a device. Each is one step of the design's steps 5 to 7.

author: blu
body: Marking a candidate resets the attempt count: this image has not had its chances yet.

author: blu
body: The decision itself, given whether the candidate's bytes verified. The primary is the answer to every doubt.

author: blu
body: A candidate that has run out of attempts or failed its hash is not merely skipped for this boot -- it is abandoned, so the next boot does not pay to hash it again forever.

author: blu
body: The flag write is the commit point and is one aligned word.

author: blu
body: Step 5. The digest and the length go down first and the flag last, in a separate cycle. Lose power in between and the next boot finds a marker that does not claim a candidate, reads no digest, and boots the firmware it already had.

author: blu
body: A candidate past its limit is not hashed. There is no point paying for a digest over an image that has already used its chances, and the answer is the same either way.

author: blu
body: Step 7. The firmware that just booted says it is healthy, and only then does the candidate become the primary.
